title: The plain meeting house
hook: Quaker and Puritan rooms of white walls and clear glass

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gothic cathedral: stone lifted high, walls turned into colored glass. Your line was stone reaching up.

White walls. Clear glass. Wooden benches. No statues, no painted windows, no altar. In a Quaker meeting house the benches may face each other, with no pulpit at all. People come in, sit down, and the room goes quiet. A clock ticks. Outside, a branch moves. After a while, someone stands, says a few sentences, and sits down. In an old New England meeting house built by Puritans, the room is just as bare, but everything turns toward a high pulpit where the Bible is read and preached. Two plain rooms, built that way on purpose.

Yesterday's cathedral asked how a building can lift the eye toward God. The meeting house, from the same Bible, asks what might stand in the way. Start with the building. In Athens, Paul tells a crowd standing among temples: "God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands." Plain builders leaned hard on that line. The room shelters the people, and that's its job. Next, the worship. Jesus tells a Samaritan woman at a well, "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." Puritans wanted worship stripped back to what they found in scripture, so the Bible, read and preached, stands at the center. Quakers went another way into the same plainness. As day two hundred seventy-nine told, they speak of the light of Christ within each person, and they hear it in John's Gospel: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." So in a Quaker meeting of the silent kind, anyone may rise and speak, and no one has to. Then, the people: "For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them." In this reading, the gathering is the room's holy center. Last, the clear glass. No saints in the window, just the real sky and the real tree. On the mountain, Elijah learns that the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire. After the fire came "a still small voice."
screen: `DWELLETH NOT IN TEMPLES MADE WITH HANDS.`

segments.voice: Find the barest spot you can, a blank wall or an empty table, and sit with nothing to look at and nothing to do, letting thoughts pass. If you pray, wait the way a Quaker meeting waits, without asking for anything, listening for a still small voice. If you don't, sit in the quiet and let the plainness be enough.
The plain meeting house. A room kept bare on purpose, so that nothing stands between the gathered people and God.
Your line: nothing between. Just the gathered people, the quiet, and the real sky. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In unprogrammed Quaker meetings, people gather in a plain room and sit in silence, and anyone may rise to speak when moved; churches in the Puritan and Reformed line gather in plain rooms centered on the reading and preaching of the Bible.

chat.says: That Quaker meeting house had no altar, no statues, nothing. Was it unfinished?
options: No, it's plain on purpose: God dwells not in temples made with hands, so nothing stands between.
Probably; the Quakers couldn't afford decorations, and they'd add them if they could.
It's bare for a season of mourning; the decorations go back up on feast days.
chat.meaning: Plain rooms are bare on purpose. Paul says God dwells not in temples made with hands, and clear glass leaves nothing between the people and God.

Quaker.meaning: one of the Friends, who worship by waiting in silence

Puritans.meaning: Protestants who wanted worship stripped back to scripture

Samaritan.meaning: the woman Jesus talks with at a well in John

Elijah.meaning: a prophet who heard God in a still small voice

notes: Quaker meetings described as 'of the silent kind' (unprogrammed); programmed Quaker meetings with pastors also exist. Confirm the framing is fair.

New England Puritan meeting houses described as plain and turned toward a high pulpit; general, undated. Confirm.
Hebrew of 1 Kings 19:12 (qol demamah daqqah) and transliteration should be checked.
The cathedral/meeting-house contrast is framed as two answers to different questions, neither ranked; confirm it reads that way.
